text: Algae range from microscopic one-celled microalgae to giant seaweeds. Some seaweeds may grow up to 160 ft (50 m) long.
Most algae live in water, especially in the sea. Most are plankton, carried along by the water, though some big seaweeds hold themselves in place with holdfasts.
Phytoplankton get their energy from sunlight, by photosynthesis, as trees and other plants do on land. So they live in the sunlit surface of oceans and lakes.
Phytoplankton are only about 1% of all the plant material on Earth. Yet they do about half of all photosynthesis and make at least half of the oxygen.
About 12,000 species of diatoms have been documented. Diatoms are phytoplankton, the most common kind of plankton.
Diatoms are tiny, generally 20 to 200 micrometers across. They form huge blooms each spring and fall, and make about half of the photosynthesis in the oceans.
Fermentation is a change made by tiny yeasts or bacteria. They turn sugars and starches into acids and other chemicals.
Yeast makes carbon dioxide gas that makes bread rise. Bacteria make lactic acid that helps keep sour foods like sauerkraut and yogurt from spoiling.
In 1856, the French chemist Louis Pasteur showed that yeast is connected to fermentation.
Cheese is made by curdling milk, usually from cows, goats or sheep. Over a thousand types of cheese exist.
Yogurt is most often made from cow's milk, but milk from water buffalo, goats, ewes, mares, camels and yaks can be used too.
Sourdough bread was carried into Alaska and the Yukon in Canada during the Klondike Gold Rush of 1898.
Antonie van Leeuwenhoek made his own microscopes, each with a single lens. He was the first person to observe and experiment with microbes.
Antonie van Leeuwenhoek wrote some 190 letters to the Royal Society about his findings. He wrote them in Dutch.
In 1665, Robert Hooke was one of the first scientists to study living things at microscopic scale. He used a compound microscope that he designed.
Louis Pasteur invented a way to treat milk so that bacteria cannot spoil it. The process is now called pasteurization.
Louis Pasteur's work is credited with saving millions of lives, through vaccines for rabies and anthrax.
In 1928, Alexander Fleming found penicillin in a mold. It has been called the greatest victory ever won over disease.
Tardigrades are usually about 0.02 in (0.5 mm) long when fully grown. Most range from 0.002 to 0.02 in (0.05 to 0.5 mm).
In 1773, a German scientist called them 'little water bears'. In 1776, an Italian scientist named them Tardigrada, which means 'slow walkers'.
About 1,500 species of tardigrades are known. They live on land, in fresh water and in the sea.
A typical house dust mite is only about 0.01 in long.
Dust mites live in the dust in homes. In a survey, dust mite allergen was found in the beds of about 84% of U.S. homes.
Rotifers are tiny animals with many cells. Scientists did not recognize them as animals until 1838, and now about 2,200 species of rotifers are known.
Dr. John Snow traced a cholera outbreak in London's Soho back to one public water pump. His work helped start the study of how diseases spread.
Snow's findings changed how London handled its water and waste. Other cities made the same changes, and public health improved around the world.
The first step in cleaning surface water is to take out big things like sticks, leaves and rubbish. They would get in the way of the later steps.
People clean water in many ways: filters, slow sand filters, chlorine, and even ultraviolet light.
Chlorine is a common disinfectant. It is used in swimming pools to keep them sanitary.
Boiling or a home filter is not always enough. Water from an unknown place can hold things that they do not remove.
Microbes have been found in sediment as hot as 248°F (120°C), 0.75 mi (1.2 km) below the sea floor.
Some microbes thrive inside rocks up to 1,900 ft (580 m) below the sea floor. Over them sits 8,500 ft (2,600 m) of ocean.
Spores from a kind of Bacillus bacteria were still alive after being heated to 788°F (420°C).
In the 1960s, scientists thought bacteria could not live above about 131°F (55°C). Soon they found many bacteria that survived and even thrived at higher temperatures.
A hot-spring bacterium called Thermus aquaticus makes an enzyme that handles heat. Scientists use it in PCR, a way to copy DNA.
Some microbes, called halophiles, grow best in very salty water, with 50 grams of salt per liter or more. A coral reef has about 35 grams per liter.
Edward Jenner, an English doctor, created the smallpox vaccine. It was the world's first vaccine.
In Jenner's time, smallpox killed around 10% of the world's people. In towns and cities, it killed as many as 20%.
A vaccine trains the body's immune system to see a germ as a threat. Then the body can destroy that germ if it meets it later.
In 1798, Edward Jenner wrote about the protective effect of cowpox against smallpox.
Penicillin was one of the first medicines that worked against many bacterial infections. In 1945, three men shared a Nobel Prize for it.
The word antibiotic was first used in 1942 by Selman Waksman and his team. They used it for any substance made by a microorganism that works against the growth of other microorganisms.
